pages.task: In the room, lamp -H1 is fixed to the frame of motor -M1. Is the lamp fed from the motor's cable?
pages.answer: No, it is fed from the isolator's line
pages.why: The lamp's line leaves through a dot on the line from -Q1. So the lamp is lit whenever -Q1 is closed, whether the motor runs or not.

pages.name: Crossings and dots
pages.text: On most diagrams, lines that cross with no dot are not joined. A dot marks a real joint, called a [[junction]]. The legend says how a sheet marks its joints. The motor's cable lights with the starter and the motor. The lamp's line crosses it with no dot, so it stays dark.

pages.name: In a row
pages.task: Three heaters are drawn in one row along the top. How are the three heaters joined?
pages.answer: -E1 in series with -E2 and -E3 in parallel
pages.why: Every path from the supply passes through -E1 first. Then it splits at the dot, through -E2 or through -E3, and joins again. Parts drawn in a row are in series only if one path runs through each in turn.

pages.name: The drawn state
pages.text: A diagram usually draws each part in one fixed state, with coils off and valves in their normal or neutral position. Good design makes that off state the safest one. So the drawing can differ from the plant as it runs. As drawn, the starter's main contact is open. Valve -V2 is shut, where its spring holds it. With the plant running, the contact is closed and -V2 is open.

pages.task: The pump is running. A contact of starter -K1, marked normally closed, is drawn closed. What is that contact doing now?
pages.why: A normally closed contact is drawn closed, with its coil off. The pump runs, so the coil of -K1 is on and that contact is open.

pages.why: The line runs to motor -M1, and through dots to -H2 and -P2. Lamp -H1's line only crosses it. So it reaches 3 parts.
